lessons.title: What's your name?
lessons.goal: Say your full name and ask for someone else's.

tip.title: Three ways to say your name
tip.body: Me llamo Ana literally means "I call myself Ana" and is the most common way. Soy Ana ("I'm Ana") is just as natural, and Mi nombre es Ana sounds a little more formal. Spanish ll sounds like the y in "yes" in most places, so llamo is "YA-mo". To spell, letters have names: te, a, i griega (y), ele, o, erre.

lines.name: Marta
lines.t: ¡Hola! Soy Marta. ¿Y tú, cómo te llamas?
lines.n: Hi! I'm Marta. And you, what's your name?

lines.t: Me llamo Alex. Mucho gusto.
lines.n: My name is Alex. Pleased to meet you.

lines.name: Marta
lines.t: Igualmente. ¿Alex es tu nombre?
lines.n: Likewise. Is Alex your first name?

lines.t: Sí. Y mi apellido es Taylor.
lines.n: Yes. And my surname is Taylor.

lines.name: Marta
lines.t: ¿Taylor? ¿Cómo se escribe?
lines.n: Taylor? How do you spell it?

lines.t: Te, a, i griega, ele, o, erre.
lines.n: T, A, Y, L, O, R.

prompts.n: Tell someone your name is Alex.
Ask a new classmate what their name is.
Ask how a name is spelt.

lessons.title: Where are you from?
lessons.goal: Say where you're from and where you live.

tip.title: Nationalities are small and change ending
tip.body: Nationalities and languages are written with a small letter: inglés, mexicana. Most have a man's form and a woman's form: un hombre es inglés, una mujer es inglesa; él es americano, ella es americana. Soy de + place (Soy de Londres) never changes, so it's the easiest way to start.

phrases.note: Same for men and women. Americano/americana is also common.

phrases.t: Soy de Manchester, pero vivo en Madrid.
phrases.n: I'm from Manchester, but I live in Madrid.

lines.name: Luis
lines.t: ¿De dónde eres?
lines.n: Where are you from?

lines.t: Soy de Inglaterra, de Manchester.
lines.n: I'm from England, from Manchester.

lines.name: Luis
lines.t: ¡Qué padre! ¿Y vives en Manchester?
lines.n: How cool! (Mexico) And do you live in Manchester?

lines.t: No, vivo en Londres. ¿Y tú?
lines.n: No, I live in London. And you?

lines.name: Luis
lines.t: Yo soy de aquí, de Oaxaca. Soy mexicano.
lines.n: I'm from here, from Oaxaca. I'm Mexican.

prompts.n: Ask a friend where they live.
Say you're from Manchester but live in Madrid.
t: Soy de Manchester pero vivo en Madrid

lessons.title: Languages
lessons.goal: Say which languages you speak and ask for help.

tip.title: español or castellano?
tip.body: Both words mean Spanish. Español is used everywhere; in Spain and parts of South America you'll also hear castellano, especially to distinguish it from Catalan, Basque or Galician. Hablo means "I speak", hablas "you speak": the h is always silent.

phrases.t: Hablo inglés y un poco de español.
phrases.n: I speak English and a little Spanish.
How do you say "bill" in Spanish?

lines.name: Jordi
lines.t: ¡Hola! ¿Hablas español?
lines.n: Hi! Do you speak Spanish?

lines.t: Un poco. Estoy aprendiendo español.
lines.n: A little. I'm learning Spanish.

lines.name: Jordi
lines.t: ¡Genial! Yo hablo español, catalán y un poco de inglés.
lines.n: Great! I speak Spanish, Catalan and a little English.

lines.t: Perdón, no entiendo. ¿Puede repetir, por favor?
lines.n: Sorry, I don't understand. Could you repeat that, please?

lines.name: Jordi
lines.t: Claro. Hablo español… catalán… e inglés.
lines.n: Sure. I speak Spanish… Catalan… and English.

lines.t: ¡Ah, vale! Gracias.
lines.n: Ah, OK! Thanks.

prompts.n: Say you speak English and a little Spanish.
t: Hablo inglés y un poco de español

prompts.n: Politely ask someone if they speak English.

lessons.title: ser: soy, eres, es…
lessons.goal: Use every form of ser, "to be".

tip.title: ser is irregular: learn it as a chant
tip.body: yo soy, tú eres, usted es, él/ella es, nosotros somos, vosotros sois, ustedes son, ellos/ellas son. Use ser for who you are: name, origin, nationality, job. Vosotros sois ("you all", informal) is only used in Spain; in Latin America ustedes son is the plural "you" for everyone. Usted and ustedes take the él/ellos forms.

phrases.note: A group of women says nosotras.
In Spain, friends say ¿Vosotros sois de aquí?

prompts.n: Say that we are from London.
Ask a group in Mexico where they're from.

lessons.title: First Spanish class
lessons.goal: Understand classmates introducing themselves at normal speed.

story.title: The first lesson in Salamanca
story.intro: On the first morning of a language course in Salamanca, the teacher asks a student to introduce himself.

lines.name: Profesora
lines.t: ¡Buenos días a todos! Bienvenidos a la clase. Me llamo Elena y soy profesora de español.
lines.n: Good morning, everyone! Welcome to the class. My name is Elena and I'm a Spanish teacher.

lines.name: Profesora
lines.t: Y tú, ¿cómo te llamas? Preséntate, por favor.
lines.n: And you, what's your name? Introduce yourself, please.

lines.name: Diego
lines.t: Hola, me llamo Diego. Soy mexicano, de Monterrey.
lines.n: Hi, my name is Diego. I'm Mexican, from Monterrey.

lines.name: Profesora
lines.t: ¡Ah! Pero tú ya hablas español.
lines.n: Oh! But you already speak Spanish.

lines.name: Diego
lines.t: Sí, claro. Soy profesor de inglés y vivo aquí desde enero. Estoy aquí para ayudar.
lines.n: Yes, of course. I'm an English teacher and I've lived here since January. I'm here to help.

lines.name: Profesora
lines.t: ¡Perfecto! Diego habla español e inglés. Somos dos profesores hoy.
lines.n: Perfect! Diego speaks Spanish and English. We're two teachers today.

lessons.title: Hotel check-in
lessons.goal: Give your name, spell it and answer questions at reception.

phrases.note: Mexico; in Spain people say Tengo una reserva.

branch.title: At reception
branch.scene: You arrive at a small hotel in Guadalajara, Mexico, in the evening.
branch.name: Recepcionista

hello.n: Good evening! How can I help you?

choices.n: Good evening. I have a reservation.

english.t: Lo siento, solo un poquito. ¿Habla usted español?
english.n: Sorry, only a tiny bit. Do you speak Spanish?

choices.t: Sí, un poco. Tengo una reservación.
choices.n: Yes, a little. I have a reservation.

lost.outcome: You gave up on Spanish and got stuck. Try again: you know enough to check in!

spell.n: Taylor? How do you spell that, please?

choices.t: Te, a, i griega, ele, o, erre.
choices.n: T, A, Y, L, O, R.

confused.t: ¿No sabe cómo se escribe su apellido?
confused.n: You don't know how to spell your surname?

passport.t: Gracias. Sí, aquí está su reservación. ¿De dónde es usted?
passport.n: Thank you. Yes, here's your reservation. Where are you from?

room.t: ¡Qué bien! Su habitación es la doce. ¡Que descanse!
room.n: How nice! Your room is number twelve. Have a good rest!
room.outcome: You checked in completely in Spanish and got your key.

prompts.n: At reception, say you have a reservation.

culture.title: tú, usted, vosotros, ustedes
culture.body: For one person, Spanish has informal tú and polite usted; Spaniards switch to tú quickly, while in much of Latin America usted lasts longer, especially with older people and in shops. For several people, Spain uses vosotros among friends and ustedes for polite situations. In Latin America (and the Canary Islands) vosotros isn't used at all: ustedes covers every group, friends included. You'll understand vosotros in films and books from Spain, but ustedes always works.

phrases.n: Shall we use tú with each other?

free.n: Introduce yourself: your name, where you're from, where you live and which languages you speak.
free.hint: Me llamo …, Soy de …, Vivo en …, Hablo inglés y un poco de español.
free.model: ¡Hola! Me llamo Alex Taylor. Soy de Inglaterra, de Manchester, pero vivo en Londres. Hablo inglés y un poco de español. Estoy aprendiendo español. ¡Mucho gusto!

prompts.n: Suggest to a new acquaintance that you use tú.
Ask a group of friends in Mexico if they're from here.
